items.title: fix(two-factor): prevent TOTP code reuse within its validity window

labels.name: security
labels.description: 2FA, rate limiting, captcha, HIBP

items.body:
## What

Enforces single-use TOTP codes per RFC 6238 §5.2 in the `twoFactor` verify path.
Evaluates the standard acceptance window `[-1, 0, 1]` with constant-time earliest-match; any replayed code is rejected with `INVALID_CODE`.

## Why

Fixes #10387:
- The same TOTP code could be replayed within its ~90s validity window for step-up, and reused across independent sign-in challenges — violating RFC 6238 §5.2 ("a verifier MUST ensure each code is used only once per time step").
- Root cause: stateless `createOTP(...).verify(code)` with no consumption record, so any valid code in-window verified indefinitely until the step expired.

## Fix

- Atomically reserves a step-keyed replay tombstone `totp-used:<twoFactorId>:<matchedStep>` via `reserveVerificationValue`, with TTL bounded to window expiry (`(matchedStep + 2) * period`).
- Secondary-storage parity via atomic increment when `verification.storeInDatabase` is not set (Redis / KV path).
- Pre-`sessionIssued` downstream failures roll back the tombstone and restore the consumed attempt (`attempt.restore`); post-`sessionIssued` failures fail closed (tombstone kept). First-verify enrollment exemption: when `twoFactor.verified !== true`, the setup code is not tombstoned so enrollment can complete.

## Linked issue

Fixes #10387.

## Follow-up

DB expired-tombstone background cleanup deferred — no sweep in this PR. Expired markers lapse via `verification.expiresAt` TTL semantics; a background reaper can be proposed separately if desired.

items.title: feat(device-authorization): support RFC 8707 resource indicators and RFC 9068 JWT access tokens

labels.name: identity
labels.description: OAuth/OIDC provider, device flow

labels.name: locked
labels.description: Locked conversations after being closed for 7 days

items.body:
The device authorization plugin could only issue opaque session tokens, which prevented device clients from requesting access tokens scoped to downstream APIs. This adds an RFC 8707 resource boundary and an RFC 9068 JWT path while preserving the existing opaque-token behavior for requests without `resource`.

## What changes

- **Authorization request**: `/device/code` accepts one or more `resource` values in JSON or form-encoded requests, preserves repeated form parameters, and binds the resolved audience to the device grant.
- **User approval**: `GET /device` returns the requesting `client_id`, `scope`, and `resource` only to the authenticated user who owns the request, so approval pages can present the complete grant before accepting it.
- **Token issuance**: `/device/token` can use the full bound resource set or request a subset. A valid resource produces an RFC 9068 JWT whose verification keys come from the JWT plugin's configured JWKS setup; the no-resource path continues creating a Better Auth session and returning its opaque token.
- **Policy controls**: `allowedResources` defines the global resource allow-list, while `onDeviceAuthRequest` can enforce client-specific resource and scope policy. Invalid targets fail before consuming an approved code, and `customAccessTokenClaims` cannot override authorization-server-owned claims.
- **Storage**: device grants persist their approved audience in the nullable `deviceCode.resource` field.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> After upgrading, run the Better Auth schema migration or generation workflow so the `deviceCode` table includes the nullable `resource` field.

## Review focus

- **Grant boundary**: the token endpoint rejects resources that were not approved at `/device/code`, and a token-time resource must be a subset of the bound grant.
- **Issuance failure**: the JWT plugin requirement and resource policy are checked before the approved code is consumed, so a configuration or request error does not force the user through another device flow.
- **Multi-audience tokens**: deployments must ensure that every requested scope has the same meaning for every resource in a multi-resource audience.

Closes #10345.

items.body: Part of #8023. Phase 1: impersonation only. Delegation (`actor_token`, `act`) and access-token `acr`/`auth_time` follow in phase 2, after #9935 and #11267. ## Summary A service that receives a user's token, such as an MCP server, can trade it for a token to another API instead of passing it through: ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant C as MCP client participant M as MCP server (confidential client) participant AS as oauth-provider participant API as Downstream API C->>M: tools/call + token (aud = MCP) M->>AS: grant_type=token-exchange, subject_token, resource=API AS-->>M: access token (sub = user, aud = API, client_id = M) M->>API: Bearer exchanged token ``` `oauthTokenExchange()` is a companion plugin registered through `extendOAuthProvider`, following the device grant. The rules it applies: - **Who may exchange:** only a confidential client registered for the grant. - **Which tokens:** only access tokens this server issued. - **Confused-deputy guard:** the caller must be the token's client or a resource server in its audience. - **No escalation:** scopes must be a subset of the subject token's and the client's. With no `scope`, the default is the subject token's scopes the client may hold. - **Targets:** named by `resource` or `audience`, each must be a registered resource linked to the client. Targets are checked before consent and the policy callback. - **Consent:** a client that does not skip consent needs the user's consent under the subject token's reference. - **Lifetime:** the exchanged token never outlives the subject token and inherits its `sid`. - **Token types:** no refresh or ID token is issued. Errors follow RFC 8693 §2.2.2. Two changes reach outside the plugin: - `issueTokens({ maxExpiresAt })` caps expiry, and refuses with `invalid_request` when the cap has already passed. - The consent reference (`postLogin.consentReferenceId`) is now an AS-owned `reference_id` claim on JWT access tokens, and introspection returns it. Exchange reads it back, so a token approved for organization A stays A after the user switches organizations. Before this, exchanged tokens dropped the reference. ## Evidence A new e2e (`token-exchange-demo.spec.ts`) runs the Next.js demo, as authorization server and MCP server, against a separate downstream API that verifies tokens through JWKS. It drives real DCR, sign-in, and consent in the browser, then: - **Before:** the downstream API rejects the MCP token with 401 `invalid_token` (wrong audience). - **After:** the MCP tool's exchanged token reaches the API with the user's `sub` and the approved organization. After the organization switch it is still Acme. After sign-out the exchange fails and introspection reports the token inactive. Each RFC 8693/9068/6749 response check is labelled with its section. Unit tests also run the consent and reference checks on Postgres and MongoDB, and the device-grant test checks `reference_id` before and after a refresh. Removing the lifetime cap, the audience binding, the consent check, the scope subset, client-scope narrowing, session binding, or reference inheritance each turns a unit test or the e2e red. ## Merge Danger **Door:** two-way. The grant does nothing until the plugin is added. The new claim can be removed later, though tokens issued meanwhile still carry it. **Blast Radius:** issuance - Deployments using `postLogin.consentReferenceId` get a visible `reference_id` claim on every JWT access token. - A `reference_id` that apps set themselves through claim callbacks is now dropped with a warning. - The authorize consent lookup now goes through a shared helper. Its behavior is unchanged and covered by the existing authorize tests. - The two demo e2e specs share one `next dev` directory, so when run in parallel locally the second waits for the first to stop its server. --- ## Summary by cubic Adds RFC 8693 token exchange so a service that receives a user's access token, such as an MCP server, can trade it for an access token to another registered API instead of forwarding the user's token. The 1.7 schema adds a required `issuer` column with no default, and `auth migrate` emits a plain `ADD COLUMN ... NOT NULL` for it. On a populated database that statement fails on SQLite, Postgres, and SQL Server, while MySQL's default `sql_mode` accepts it, fills the column with an empty string on every existing row, and then builds the compound unique index over those values. The planner now refuses to generate this statement class for any populated table, so every dialect gets the same actionable error instead of a crash or a silent success.

## What changes

- `getMigrations` stops with a `BetterAuthError` when a required column with no default targets a table that has rows. The message names the physical column and table, and links the upgrade guide's backfill section only when the column is the account table's `issuer`.
- `auth generate` still emits the statements, since its output feeds external migration tools, and prefixes a comment banner naming each column that needs a manual backfill first.
- A required field whose live column is nullable logs a warning instead of failing the plan.
- The CLI awaits command actions and prints `BetterAuthError` messages cleanly, so refusals exit 1 instead of surfacing as unhandled promise rejections.
- The upgrade guide adds the MySQL self-check, the index-drop ordering for databases already affected, and the per-dialect `NOT NULL` statements that step 5 of the backfill left implicit.

The guard resolves physical names through `getAuthTables`, so custom `modelName` and field renames are honored, and it shares the column builder's default-detection predicates so the refusal and the emitted SQL cannot disagree.

items.body:
Populated Better Auth 1.6 databases need data-aware decisions for account identity, OAuth records, and SCIM state before the 1.7 schema can be applied safely. This adds a read-only planning workflow and an explicit apply step so operators can review those decisions before any data changes.

> [!WARNING]
> The guided migration can revoke or retire OAuth and SCIM state. Back up the database, stop every authentication and provisioning writer, and test the migration on a copy before applying it in production.

## Command contract

`auth migrate plan [migration-file]` inspects the database without writing. `auth migrate apply [migration-file]` reruns the same preflight, refuses every non-ready plan, and then performs the approved cutover. Only `apply` accepts non-interactive approval. Both commands support deterministic JSON output, while plain `auth migrate` remains a deprecated alias for `auth migrate apply`.

## Account identity preflight

| Database state | Configuration | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Empty | Explicit provider-id or issuer | Ready |
| Empty | Omitted | Ready under issuer compatibility behavior, with the explicit configuration recommendation |
| Populated 1.6 | Omitted | Blocked; configure `account: { identityStrategy: "provider-id" }` |
| Populated 1.6 | Explicit provider-id | Checks `(providerId, accountId)` collisions, backfills deterministic namespaces, and enforces the v1.7 schema |
| Populated 1.6 | Explicit issuer | Blocked; authority adoption requires a separately reviewed re-key migration |
| Populated v1.7 issuer | Omitted or explicit issuer | Account identity is a no-op; omission retains the compatibility warning |
| Populated v1.7 issuer | Explicit provider-id | Blocked as an unsafe re-key request |
| Populated provider-id synthetic | Explicit provider-id | No-op |
| Populated provider-id synthetic | Omitted or explicit issuer | Blocked with the exact provider-id configuration to restore |

Partial backfills, malformed reserved namespaces, and collisions fail with account counts, affected providers, and corrective next steps. Startup never scans the database or infers a cohort; this classification belongs only to migration preflight.

Both strategies retain required `issuer`, required `accountId`, and the unique `(issuer, accountId)` index. For provider-id migration, the guided path persists deterministic namespaces such as `local:oauth:google`; it does not repurpose `providerId` as a remote issuer.

## Plan evidence and other release state

- Reports selected and detected strategies, total and external account counts, automatic namespace resolution, and projected collisions. This folds in the readiness reporting previously proposed in #10970.
- Moves OAuth clients and eligible consents, hashes secrets when selected, and revokes retired provider tokens.
- Inventories legacy SCIM provider-owned accounts, retires approved rows, and records the reprovisioning boundary.
- Stores reviewed release choices in `better-auth-migration.json` and blocks when the database or configuration no longer matches them.
- Honors custom SQL table and column names through built-in, Drizzle, and Prisma migration connections.

MySQL validates deterministic failures before writes and uses resumable checkpoints around implicitly committing schema operations. PostgreSQL, SQLite, and SQL Server keep supported work on a scoped migration connection and use native transaction behavior where available.


After a successful apply, retained 1.6 backup tables count as completed checkpoints only when the reviewed OAuth and SCIM work is already reflected in the target state. A repeated plan is then up to date, while incomplete MySQL checkpoints remain resumable.

items.body:
Provider Accounts currently combine durable upstream identity ownership with provider-configuration credentials and lifecycle state. This separates those boundaries so a trusted Identity can survive configuration changes without allowing credentials, tokens, or provider deletion to cross provider instances. ## What changes - **Identity ownership:** the new `Identity` model owns `(issuer, providerAccountId)` and links that provider-side subject to one User. - **Provider Accounts:** each Account points to an Identity and owns configuration-specific credentials, grants, tokens, and lifecycle state under `(identityId, providerInstanceId)`. - **SSO isolation:** persisted providers receive immutable instance namespaces; callbacks fail closed when the provider changes in flight, and deletion removes only that instance's Accounts. - **Portable lifecycle:** multi-record identity changes commit through an interactive transaction or an adapter-provided atomic batch. Account-owned plugin records are removed consistently without relying on foreign-key cascades. - **Public contracts:** Account responses nest their Identity, Generic OAuth exposes identity-named resolvers, SIWE wallet metadata belongs to its Account, and SCIM contributes a typed `connectionId` to `validateUserInfo`. > [!IMPORTANT] > This is a breaking schema and adapter change. Existing installations must backfill the Identity table, Account identity and provider-instance keys, and SIWE wallet ownership before deploying. Custom adapters need an interactive transaction or `commitAtomicWrites`; dynamically registered SSO providers specifically require interactive transactions. Drizzle integrations must declare `transaction: "async"`, `"sync"`, or `false` for their driver. SCIM remains a provisioning boundary: provisioning a User does not create a sign-in Account or infer identity ownership by email.
Architecture and failure-handling invariants - Identity ownership is unique by `(issuer, providerAccountId)`. - Provider credentials and lifecycle are unique by `(identityId, providerInstanceId)`. - `providerId` remains the public routing alias; `providerInstanceId` stays server-only. - Provider-account cookies bind to the exact session, Account, Identity, and provider instance. - Database-backed verification consumption commits its winner gate and captured sibling invalidation together. - Persisted SSO provider mutation and authentication serialize inside one native transaction.
--- ## Summary by cubic Separates durable provider identities from provider‑scoped accounts, resolves tokens and account info by provider instance (not alias), and adds a `provider_account_binding` cookie that binds Account/Identity to the exact session. Also requests TikTok identity scopes by default, keeps provider bindings on same‑user refresh, and hardens identity lifecycle edge cases. - **New Features** - Identity/Account split: `Identity` owns `(issuer, providerAccountId, userId)`; each `Account` is scoped by `(identityId, providerInstanceId)` (server‑only). APIs return `account.identity`; client `listAccounts` returns public Account/Identity fields and infers additional fields with `inferAdditionalFields`. - Stronger SSO isolation: tokens and account‑info resolve from `providerInstanceId` instead of `providerId`; providers without an issuer use `local:oauth:`; deleting a provider removes only its Accounts. A new `provider_account_binding` cookie ties the session, Account, Identity, and provider instance, and is preserved on same‑user session/profile refresh. The encrypted `account_data` cookie is supported when `account.storeAccountCookie` is enabled and follows the cookie cache lifetime. TikTok now requires a stable `union_id` subject and requests `user.info.basic` and `user.info.profile` by default. - Adapters & atomicity: interactive transactions by default or adapter‑provided `commitAtomicWrites` for Cloudflare D1. Drizzle declares `transaction: "async" | "sync" | false`; Prisma and Kysely use interactive transactions; Kysely on D1 accepts a `d1Database` binding; MongoDB enables native transactions by passing a connected `MongoClient` (replica set/sharded required). SCIM requires native interactive transactions. - OAuth/Plugins & contracts: Generic OAuth switches to `identityIssuer`/`identitySubject` with `OAuthIdentityKeyContext`; identity recognition via `resolveOAuthIdentityKey`. SIWE wallet metadata is now account‑owned. Session `userId` FK is `onDelete: "restrict"`. Client docs show `{ data, error }` patterns for token APIs. - Edge‑case hardening: explicit cleanup for account‑owned plugin records; more robust verification reservation/consume flow (lock retries); correct MSSQL mapping for `onDelete: "restrict"`; improved nested endpoint error propagation; safer cookie binding rotation. - **Migration** - Backfill `identity` rows; set `account.identityId` and `account.providerInstanceId`; add unique `(identityId, providerInstanceId)` and related indexes. Change session FK to `onDelete: "restrict"`. Move SIWE `walletAddress.userId` to `walletAddress.accountId`. - Rename Generic OAuth config from `accountIssuer`/`accountSubject` to `identityIssuer`/`identitySubject`; update code reading identity fields; replace adapter calls with `createUserWithAccount` and `linkAccount`. - Ensure atomic lifecycles: enable interactive transactions or implement `commitAtomicWrites` (D1). ## Summary

Add an optional `validateRedirectUri` callback to the OAuth provider for deployments with dynamic callback URIs, such as preview hosts controlled by the application operator. Existing configurations continue to use registered URI matching and native loopback port variance. This is a patch changeset because no existing configuration needs to change.

## Behavior

The callback receives the requested URI, the client's registered URIs, and the result of the default validation. It can extend, restrict, or replace that result. The provider consults it both when authorizing a redirect and when deciding whether an early authorization error can be returned to that URI. A rejected or throwing callback falls back to the server error page. URI syntax, fragments, credentials, and unsafe schemes cannot be approved by the callback.

Client registration is unchanged. Clients created through the built-in endpoints still need a concrete redirect URI.

## Security considerations

Accepting dynamic callback hosts relaxes the exact URI matching recommended by RFC 9700. Operators must constrain the scheme, hostname, port, path, and query, and ensure that untrusted contributors cannot deploy under an accepted hostname. The documentation includes a constrained preview-host example and explains how custom-validated hosts affect pairwise subject identifiers.

items.body:
Better Auth currently looks only at the database type to decide if it should handle timestams as Date or string.
This PR extends this feature to allow customizing this behavior:

```ts
    // Force timestamp-like types to be returned as raw strings
    // to preserve full precision for downstream consumers
    types: {
      // PostgreSQL OIDs for timestamp-related types
      timestamptz: { from: [1184], to: 1184, parse: (s: string) => s, serialize: (s: string) => s },
      timestamp: { from: [1114], to: 1114, parse: (s: string) => s, serialize: (s: string) => s },
      date: { from: [1082], to: 1082, parse: (s: string) => s, serialize: (s: string) => s },
      time: { from: [1083], to: 1083, parse: (s: string) => s, serialize: (s: string) => s },
      timetz: { from: [1266], to: 1266, parse: (s: string) => s, serialize: (s: string) => s },
    },

    // later on I init betterAuth:
  export const auth = betterAuth({
  // Use Better Auth's Kysely adapter with supportsDates: false for Neon compatibility
  // This prevents crashes when the database driver returns dates as strings
  database: kyselyAdapter(db, {
    type: 'postgres',
    supportsDates: false, // NEW: Fix for Neon/PostgreSQL driver returning dates as strings
  }),
```

Without that, I get `ERROR [Better Auth]: Failed to create user TypeError [ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE]: The "string" argument must be of type string or an instance of Buffer or ArrayBuffer. Received an instance of Date`

Took me quite some time to debug, I used AI to write this fix, so the tests defo need work,
but I wanted to get the discussion going first if this is something you consider.

And since I'm fairly new to web tech, also if this pattern is common.
I did talk with @igalklebanov and he confirmed that this is a common pattern.


Alternative design if we wanna be even more explicit (but then I'd expect auto to do a one-time probe)
```ts
  dates: 'auto',           // default
  // dates: 'native',     // force Date passthrough
  // dates: 'string',     // force ISO strings at DB boundary
```

Why go in on all strings?
This allows my project to keep full precision on time and greatly simplify date/time conversion.
Everything is a zod-verified timestamp, date conversion happens at the UI layer.
Especially with React RSC that's super nice, so I can push my existing models to the frontend.

Why not read from the db layer?
I considered reading the config from the database but that gets messy fast - I use Neon in prod which again has a differert type configuration syntax - so a new option seemed easier.

No conversion?
I use `postgres.js` which returns [correct ISO 8601](https://github.com/porsager/postgres/blob/32feb259a3c9abffab761bd1758b3168d9e0cebc/src/types.js#L31), as does Neon. pg returns ISO (with a space instead of T + numeric offset) so folks using that still have to do a tiny conversion or a [json_object trick](https://onecompiler.com/postgresql/43v4ab5kn) to get ISO 8601.
    
<!-- This is an auto-generated description by cubic. -->
---

## Summary by cubic
Adds a supportsDates option to the Kysely adapter to control how date/time fields are handled. This prevents crashes with drivers that return strings (e.g., Neon Postgres) and allows preserving full timestamp precision by using ISO strings.

- **New Features**
  - New config: supportsDates. When false, dates are handled as strings. Defaults remain: sqlite/mssql=false, postgres/mysql=true. Can be overridden per adapter.
  - Added tests to cover defaults and overrides.

- **Migration**
  - If your Postgres driver returns dates as strings (e.g., Neon), set supportsDates: false in kyselyAdapter({ type: 'postgres', supportsDates: false }).

<!-- End of auto-generated description by cubic. -->

items.body: Closes #10748 ## Context `user.deleteUser` already supports an optional email-confirmation step before deleting an account (`sendDeleteAccountVerification`). The organization plugin has no equivalent for its two most destructive, effectively irreversible actions: deleting an organization, and reassigning ownership. This PR brings both in line with that existing pattern, plus a follow-up: making the emailed confirmation link itself non-destructive to open, across all four surfaces where one now exists. **Authorization to open this PR:** explicit go-ahead from **@max** (ping-maxwell) on Discord. At the time of writing, the issue is still untriaged on GitHub (no `target:*` label, no maintainer response on the thread yet). Happy to adjust scope or close this if the direction doesn't match what the team has in mind. ## What this PR adds **Organization deletion confirmation** - `organizationDeletion.sendDeleteOrganizationVerification` gates `organization.delete` behind a confirmation email. The token is a JSON payload (`organizationId`, requesting user id), validated with zod on read, single-use, scoped to that pair. - New `GET /organization/delete/callback` re-validates session and the `organization:delete` permission (both may have changed since the email was sent), then atomically consumes the token *immediately before* applying the deletion. Resolving the token (session, membership, permission checks) and consuming it are deliberately separate steps, so a visit to the link that can't complete the deletion — no session, wrong session, permission since revoked — never burns the token first; the real user can still use it afterwards. The existing deletion path runs unchanged, including `beforeDeleteOrganization`/`afterDeleteOrganization`. **Ownership transfer** - New `POST /organization/transfer-ownership`, deliberately not folded into `update-member-role` (which stays generic and synchronous). Callable only by a member who currently holds the creator role — the same rule `update-member-role` already enforces specifically for touching that role, rather than the broader `member:update` permission (which the built-in `admin` role also holds, and which has no business authorizing a role reassignment this consequential on its own). - `adapter.transferOwnership` atomically promotes the target and demotes the current owner inside a transaction. The demotion is a guarded update — conditioned on the owner still holding the exact role read moments earlier, the same pattern this file already uses for `updateInvitation`'s `fromStatus` guard — so two concurrent transfers initiated by the same owner toward different targets can result in at most one actually applying. - `ownershipTransfer.sendTransferOwnershipVerification` gates it behind a confirmation email sent to the **current owner** (they're the one giving up control, not the target), with the same resolve-then-consume token handling as organization deletion, and new `beforeTransferOwnership`/`afterTransferOwnership` hooks. **`confirmationMode: "instant" | "explicit"`** (default `"instant"`), on all four surfaces (`user.deleteUser`, `user.changeEmail`, `organizationDeletion`, `ownershipTransfer`) - Today, the emailed link for all of these is a plain `GET` that applies the change on visit. Some email clients and security scanners open links automatically to scan them (Outlook Safe Links, link-preview proxies), which can trigger the change without the user actually clicking anything. - In `"explicit"` mode, the emailed `url` points at the app's own callback URL with the token attached instead of better-auth's endpoint, and a `.../preview` (GET, no mutation) + `.../confirm` (POST, applies it) pair replaces the single destructive GET. - All four `.../preview` and `.../confirm` endpoints require an authenticated session matching the pending change, and bypass the cookie cache on stateful deployments for that check. This is deliberately *not* the same contract as the pre-existing instant `/verify-email` GET callback, which is a direct browser link click and may legitimately arrive with no session (clicked from a device the user isn't logged in on) — these four are meant to be called by the app's own confirmation page, often server-side with no end-user session forwarded at all, so they reject cleanly instead of minting a session nobody asked for. - Default stays `"instant"` everywhere, so this is fully backward compatible. Both organization features and `confirmationMode` are opt-in: without configuring the relevant callback, behavior is unchanged. ## Things worth flagging in review - **`organization.delete`'s response type is now a union** (`Organization | { success, message }`), to accommodate the pending-verification acknowledgement — mirrors `deleteUser`'s existing contract, but it's a type change for `authClient.organization.delete`'s callers even when they don't use the new option. Called out in the changeset as a types-only breaking change. - **`changeEmail`'s token isn't single-use.** It's a signed JWT, not a `verification` DB row, so a `/change-email/confirm` replay after the first successful application fails with "User not found" (the token's lookup key is the pre-change email, which no longer belongs to any user) rather than being cleanly rejected as invalid. This is pre-existing behavior of the instant-mode link too, not introduced here — documented explicitly in `docs/content/docs/concepts/users-accounts.mdx`. - **Naming collision with an existing option.** The organization plugin already has a top-level `disableOrganizationDeletion: boolean`. This PR introduces a differently-shaped, nested `organizationDeletion` option for the confirmation config. Happy to rename either if the team would rather avoid the near-collision. ## Testing - New tests across `update-user.test.ts`, `crud-org.test.ts`, and a new `transfer-ownership.test.ts` cover: back-compat with no configuration, instant and explicit confirmation for all four surfaces, single-use token races (concurrent callbacks with the same token apply at most once), cross-organization token scoping, a non-owner admin being rejected from transferring ownership, concurrent transfers to different targets resolving to exactly one owner, permission revoked between send and confirm, `deleteUser`'s optional password re-check at confirm time, and hook firing. - `pnpm typecheck` passes. - Full existing suites re-run clean: `packages/better-auth/src/api` and `packages/better-auth/src/plugins/organization`, 710 tests total across both, including the new ones. ## Docs Updated `docs/content/docs/plugins/organization.mdx` (delete confirmation, new Transfer Ownership section, Options list, `` schemas kept in sync with the actual zod bodies) and `docs/content/docs/concepts/users-accounts.mdx` (`confirmationMode` for `deleteUser`/`changeEmail`, the session requirement on the preview/confirm endpoints, the JWT replay caveat), plus the coarse `reference/options.mdx` sample. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_01U3d98r2fYSginqYX37zbhh --- ## Summary by cubic Adds opt-in email confirmation for organization deletion and a new `organization.transferOwnership` endpoint, plus an `"explicit"` confirmation mode for `user.deleteUser`, `user.changeEmail`, and the two new organization confirmations. In `"explicit"` mode, the emailed link previews the pending change instead of applying it, so mail clients and security scanners that auto-open links can't trigger it; a separate authenticated confirm call is required. Default stays `"instant"` everywhere, so behavior is unchanged without configuration. Closes #10748. **New Features** - `organizationDeletion.sendDeleteOrganizationVerification` gates `organization.delete` behind a single-use confirmation email; a new `GET /organization/delete/callback` resolves session and permission before consuming the token, so an unauthorized visit never burns it. - New `POST /organization/transfer-ownership` lets the current owner promote a target member; `adapter.transferOwnership` atomically promotes the target and demotes the owner inside a transaction, with a guarded update so concurrent transfers can only produce one winner. - `ownershipTransfer.sendTransferOwnershipVerification` gates it behind a confirmation email sent to the current owner, with `beforeTransferOwnership`/`afterTransferOwnership` hooks. - All four surfaces accept `confirmationMode: "explicit"`; the preview/confirm endpoints require an authenticated session matching the pending change and bypass the cookie cache on stateful deployments. **Breaking Change** - `organization.delete`'s return type is now `Organization | { success: true; message: string }` to accommodate the pending-verification response. Callers that read properties like `.slug` directly without narrowing need a type guard. Written for commit c287a2f87dd13d0d2295d57f4d548d0ce6b12184. Summary will update on new commits.

OAuth account identity currently depends on a local provider configuration and a provider-supplied identifier. The same OpenID Connect identity can split across aliases, equal identifiers from different authorities can collide, and credential identity can depend on a mutable email address.

This change gives every account an explicit, stable identity boundary.

## What changes

- **Identity key**: external accounts use the unique `(issuer, providerAccountId)` pair.
- **Account selection**: `Account.id` remains the local row selector for account-management APIs.
- **Trusted provider data**: OAuth identity resolves from verified OIDC `sub` or signed SAML `NameID`, rather than user-profile mapping.
- **Credential accounts**: credentials use the stable `(local:credential, user.id)` key.
- **Provider contracts**: Generic OAuth defaults to `sub` for OIDC discovery and `id` for plain OAuth, with explicit overrides for non-standard providers.
- **Coverage**: workflow, raw HTTP, adapter, OpenAPI, and type-contract tests verify the boundary.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> This is a breaking schema and API change. Existing account rows require a reviewed issuer backfill before the compound unique index can be enabled. The changeset and 1.7 upgrade guide define the migration contract.

<details>
<summary>Review details</summary>

- The provider-side `Account.accountId` field becomes `providerAccountId`, and `issuer` is required.
- OAuth providers resolve `accountSubject` and `accountIssuer` from raw provider data, not `mapProfileToUser`.
- Token and profile APIs require either the local account row `id` or `{ useAccountCookie: true }`; `providerId` is not an account selector.
- Provider discovery rejects malformed JWKS URLs during initialization rather than silently disabling verification.
- Direct sign-in and linking return stable authentication errors when they cannot derive a valid issuer or subject.
- Provider aliases share one account row and token set. Independent OAuth grants and provider lifecycle records are outside this change.

</details>

Closes #10214

items.body:
## Summary

Two separate bugs on the consent accept path into `authorizeEndpoint`, both reachable from the #9261 thread's multi-tenant + forced-reauth setup.

### 1. `prompt=login` honored across consent continuation

Consent accept stripped `prompt=login` unconditionally, letting a pre-existing session satisfy a forced reauthentication request. Now threads the signed request issue time (`ba_iat`) through state and only clears `prompt=login` when the active session was created at or after that time; otherwise bounces back to `/authorize`.

### 2. `postLogin.shouldRedirect` no longer re-triggers after consent

Consent accept called `authorizeEndpoint` without signaling that `postLogin` had already been cleared, so the post-consent pass re-evaluated `postLogin.shouldRedirect`. Any `shouldRedirect` implementation that can return true after postLogin completed (typical of `setActive`-driven flows where the persisted session state is not visible to the consent request) bounced the user back to the postLogin page.

`authorize` now records a `ba_pl=1` marker in the signed query it emits past the postLogin gate. Consent accept bypasses `postLogin.shouldRedirect` only when the incoming signed query carries that marker; otherwise it re-enters `authorize` with the postLogin check intact. This preserves the legitimate `setActive` → consent → code flow and blocks a direct POST to `/oauth2/consent` with a pre-postLogin signed query from skipping `shouldRedirect` to issue a code.

items.body:
Closes #8952

## Problem

The Expo client writes session data to SecureStore (`${storagePrefix}_session_data`) after every successful `/get-session` response, but never reads it back on startup. This causes the session atom to always initialize as `{ data: null, isPending: true }`, resulting in a login screen flash for returning users until the `/get-session` network request completes.

## Solution

Read the cached session data from SecureStore in `getActions` and hydrate the session atom with it as an optimistic value (stale-while-revalidate). The cached data is validated before use:

- Must contain valid `session.id` and `user.id`
- Must not be expired (checks `session.expiresAt`)
- Respects `disableCache` option
- Skipped on web (SecureStore is native-only)

The atom is set with `isPending: true` so the `/get-session` network request still runs and replaces the cached data with the fresh server response.

## Tests

Added 4 test cases covering:
- Hydration from valid cached session data
- No hydration when cache is empty
- No hydration when cached session is expired
- No hydration when `disableCache` is `true`

items.body:
SCIM provisioning was coupled to the organization plugin, so directory-owned resources inherited an application-specific tenancy and role model. This rebuild makes canonical SCIM resources connection-owned and moves user linking, lifecycle, and application access into explicit identity and projection boundaries.

[scim-demo-workflow.webm](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/498b7aaf-ad89-4202-827c-d65fa5e5280b)

## What changes

- **Connection ownership**: `scim({ connections })` defines bearer-authenticated, isolated resource owners, while provisioning domains let several connections contribute to one application boundary.
- **Identity boundary**: `identity.resolveUser` makes create-or-link decisions explicit, and `identity.reconcileUser` applies combined lifecycle state without guessing by email or creating a sign-in method.
- **Access boundary**: projections translate Group sources into validated, source-aware role grants and reconcile the complete desired state without overwriting access owned elsewhere.
- **Protocol surface**: Users, Groups, discovery, filtering, pagination, response attributes, and ordered atomic PATCH behavior are rebuilt around the new model. No-op PATCH requests now succeed.
- **Transaction semantics**: canonical writes and application callbacks commit atomically; cache and session side effects wait until commit and are discarded on rollback.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> This is a breaking SCIM cutover. The old configuration, client APIs, management surface, and organization-backed schema are removed, and existing provisioning state cannot migrate in place. Deployments must pause provisioning, replace the legacy schema, enable native interactive transactions, configure stable connections, and fully reprovision before resuming traffic. Cloudflare D1 cannot provide the required transaction behavior.
>
> Provisioned users also need a separate sign-in method. The plugin never links existing Better Auth Users by email; retaining them requires an explicit `identity.resolveUser` mapping before reprovisioning.

<details>
<summary>Review map and implementation detail</summary>

- **Ownership and lifecycle**: connection binding, identity resolution and tombstones, multi-source active state, and irreversible connection decommissioning.
- **Projection and authorization**: role allowlisting, source-aware grant ownership, complete-state reconciliation, and replay when mappings change.
- **Protocol interoperability**: public discovery, SCIM error and media envelopes, equality filters, response attributes, and Microsoft Entra ID and Okta membership PATCH shapes.
- **End-to-end workflow**: shared adapter-backed HTTP coverage and the Next.js directory workspace exercise the same provisioning path through real requests, storage, authorization checks, and UI state.
- **Migration contract**: the SCIM section of the 1.7 upgrade guide and the new reference docs define the cutover, supported surface, and explicit exclusions.

</details>

## Closed work

Closes #8549, #10398, and #10419.

Supersedes #8650, #8841, #10399, and #10420.

# Releases
## better-auth@1.7.0-beta.5

### Minor Changes

-   [#9930](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/9930) [`0cbaf81`](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/commit/0cbaf81bed9dec4c56880ee78a532262386e1ec5) Thanks [@gustavovalverde](https://github.com/gustavovalverde)! - Anonymous account linking now works after social and generic OAuth sign-in in Expo and other in-app browsers, where the OAuth callback returns without the session cookie. `onLinkAccount` fires and the anonymous user is migrated; before, it was silently skipped.

    Plugins can now carry server-trusted data across an OAuth redirect with the new `addOAuthServerContext` API, read back on the callback via `getOAuthState().serverContext`. Unlike `additionalData`, it cannot be set from the request body, so it is the right place for values the server must trust.

    For `@better-auth/oauth-provider`, the post-login authorization query now travels through that server-only channel, so it can no longer be injected through `additionalData`.

-   [#9645](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/9645) [`e014029`](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/commit/e0140297a59ddb59cccbcb4ba46c513de8cb86a7) Thanks [@ping-maxwell](https://github.com/ping-maxwell)! - Harden the Electron OAuth flow and tighten custom-scheme trusted-origin matching.

    The Electron sign-in flow now mandates PKCE S256. Plain PKCE is rejected: the `code_challenge_method` parameter is gone and every authorization code is verified by hashing the verifier with SHA-256. The server no longer trusts an `electron-origin` header to set the request Origin. The Electron client now sends a real `Origin` (for example `myapp:/`), so upgrade the `@better-auth/electron` client and server together and make sure your app's scheme is in `trustedOrigins`. The unused `disableOriginOverride` option is removed.

    Custom-scheme entries in `trustedOrigins` now match by scheme and authority instead of string prefix. A host-less entry such as `myapp://` or `exp://` still trusts every host of that scheme, but a host-bearing entry such as `myapp://callback` matches that host exactly, so it is no longer satisfied by `myapp://callback.attacker.tld`.

-   [#9966](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/9966) [`ec8a38c`](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/commit/ec8a38c08f5cfe2d922be0f8a49f2d0fa84de799) Thanks [@gustavovalverde](https://github.com/gustavovalverde)! - genericOAuth providers configured with a `discoveryUrl` now verify the provider's `id_token` against its published JWKS (signature, issuer, audience, and advertised algorithms). A sign-in whose `id_token` fails verification is rejected.

    These providers also accept client-submitted id_token sign-in through `signIn.social({ idToken })`, which previously returned `ID_TOKEN_NOT_SUPPORTED`.

    Providers configured with explicit endpoints instead of `discoveryUrl` are unchanged.

-   [#9828](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/9828) [`4f53b61`](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/commit/4f53b61f49b470a40ccab18fe1fe4d80f225905f) Thanks [@gustavovalverde](https://github.com/gustavovalverde)! - Verify social-provider id_tokens with a single shared verifier.

    Client-submitted id_token sign-in (`signIn.social({ idToken })` and account linking) is verified by one function instead of a per-provider `verifyIdToken` method. Each provider declares an `idToken` config with a JWKS source, issuer, and audience, and the core verifier runs the signature, issuer, audience, and nonce checks. A provider that declares no config rejects the client id_token path.

    PayPal previously accepted any decodable id_token without verifying its signature. PayPal derives identity from the access token, so it now declares no `idToken` config, and the client id_token path returns `ID_TOKEN_NOT_SUPPORTED`. PayPal sign-in through the redirect flow is unchanged.

    Custom providers that implement `UpstreamProvider` directly replace the removed `verifyIdToken` method with an `idToken` config:

    ```ts
    idToken: {
    	jwks: createRemoteJWKSet(new URL("https://issuer.example/.well-known/jwks.json")),
    	issuer: "https://issuer.example",
    	audience: clientId,
    },
    ```

    For verification that cannot use a local JWKS, pass `idToken: { verify: async (token, nonce) => boolean }`. The `verifyIdToken` and `disableIdTokenSignIn` provider options are unchanged.

-   [#9929](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/9929) [`91f235f`](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/commit/91f235f8604cd432749adf18c7bd7d658aa1519b) Thanks [@gustavovalverde](https://github.com/gustavovalverde)! - Add `requireEmailVerification` to OAuth provider options, for built-in social providers and the Generic OAuth plugin. When a provider reports an unverified email, the user and account are still created or linked, but no session is issued: the OAuth callback redirects with `?error=email_not_verified`, and ID token and One Tap sign-in return `403` `EMAIL_NOT_VERIFIED`. Verification emails follow the existing `emailVerification.sendOnSignUp` / `sendOnSignIn` settings.

    It is opt-in per provider and does not inherit `emailAndPassword.requireEmailVerification`, so existing social logins keep working. The gate checks the local user's verification state, so a user verified through another method keeps access. Only enable it for providers that report a trustworthy `email_verified` signal.

-   [#9969](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/9969) [`76a3342`](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/commit/76a33429fc2a3edcc85307bf81b9d92a95f9de6c) Thanks [@gustavovalverde](https://github.com/gustavovalverde)! - Signing out with `secondaryStorage` and `session.preserveSessionInDatabase` now runs your configured `session.delete` hooks and marks the preserved session row as ended. # PR Summary — Soft Delete Support for Users

Adds opt-in **soft delete** support for users. Instead of hard-deleting the user row, Better Auth anonymizes the record and sets a `deletedAt` timestamp — preserving referential integrity with related tables (posts, orders, audit logs, etc.) while fully revoking access.

---

## How to Enable

```ts title="auth.ts"
export const auth = betterAuth({
  user: {
    deleteUser: {
      enabled: true,
      softDelete: true, // new
    },
  },
});
```

---

## Behaviour

- All three deletion paths (self-delete immediate, self-delete with email confirmation, admin `removeUser`) route through `internalAdapter.deleteUser` and respect the flag — no per-path changes needed.

- Anonymization overwrites email, name, and image with safe placeholder values.

  **Default strategy:**
  - email → `deleted-{userId}@deleted.invalid` (unique per user, RFC-reserved TLD)
  - name → `"Deleted User"`
  - image → `null`

- A custom `anonymizeUser` callback can be provided to override the defaults.

- Sessions and credential/OAuth accounts are always removed regardless of soft/hard delete.

- Sign-in is blocked for soft-deleted users via a `session.create.before` database hook — returns `403 FORBIDDEN` with code `USER_DELETED`.

---

## Admin Plugin Additions

- New `POST /admin/restore-user` endpoint — clears `deletedAt`, re-enabling sign-in.
  - Requires the `user:restore` permission (admin role only).

- `listUsers` gains an `includeDeleted` boolean query parameter (default: `false`)
  - Soft-deleted users are excluded unless explicitly requested.

---

## Changes

| Area | What changed |
|------|-------------|
| packages/core | `deletedAt` added to `userSchema`; `softDelete` + `anonymizeUser` options added to `user.deleteUser`; `USER_DELETED` error code added |
| packages/better-auth | Soft delete logic in `internalAdapter.deleteUser`; sign-in block hook in `helpers.ts` |
| packages/better-auth/plugins/admin | `deletedAt` schema field; "restore" permission; `YOU_ARE_NOT_ALLOWED_TO_RESTORE_USERS` error code; `restoreUser` endpoint; `includeDeleted` query param in `listUsers` |
| docs | Soft delete section added to `users-accounts.mdx` |
| tests | 7 new tests covering all soft delete scenarios (79/79 passing) |

---

## Notes

- Restoring a user clears `deletedAt` only — original PII (email, name, image) is gone and cannot be recovered.
- Admins should re-onboard the user if needed.

- The `deletedAt` column is added to the user table via the standard schema migration:

```bash
pnpm dlx @better-auth/cli migrate
```

Implements [Client ID Metadata Documents](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document/) (draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document) for verified dynamic client discovery. This is the mechanism [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/basic/authorization#client-id-metadata-documents-flow) uses for authorization servers to discover clients without prior registration.

## New option: `clientIdMetadataDocument`

When enabled, clients can use an HTTPS URL as their `client_id`. The server fetches and validates the metadata document at that URL, creating a client automatically on first authorization request.

```ts
oauthProvider({
  clientIdMetadataDocument: {
    refreshRate: "60m",
    originBoundFields: ["redirect_uris", "post_logout_redirect_uris", "client_uri"],
    onClientCreated({ client, metadata, ctx }) { },
    onClientRefreshed({ client, metadata, ctx }) { },
  },
})
```

Configuration:
- `refreshRate`: TTL before re-fetching (default `"60m"`, accepts seconds or duration strings)
- `originBoundFields`: fields whose URLs must share the client_id origin (localhost always allowed for native app flows)
- `onClientCreated` / `onClientRefreshed`: lifecycle hooks for post-processing (trust levels, logo prefetching, change detection)

Supports `token_endpoint_auth_method: "none"` and `"private_key_jwt"` (with `jwks` or `jwks_uri`).

## Security

- SSRF protection: private/reserved IP ranges (RFC 6890), IPv4-mapped IPv6, cloud metadata endpoints; runtime-agnostic (no `node:dns`)
- Spec compliance: `client_id` must equal fetch URL, no shared secrets, no symmetric auth methods, path required, no fragments/credentials/dot-segments
- Origin-bound fields prevent cross-domain redirect URI injection
- Admin-only fields (`skip_consent`, `enable_end_session`, `disabled`) stripped from external documents
- Only recognized RFC 7591 fields persisted; arbitrary fields discarded
- 5 KB response size limit, 5-second fetch timeout, no redirect following

## Demo

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/abee40ad-04a6-4ca4-915b-f3511b3fb73d

Closes #7184

- Fix auth_time claim in ID tokens to remain stable across refresh token grants, per https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html#RefreshTokenResponse
 - Previously, auth_time was derived from ctx.context.session at token creation time, which falls back to "now" during refresh (no session in context), causing auth_time to drift on each refresh
- Now auth_time is captured from the session during authorization, stored in the verification value, persisted on the refresh token record, and carried forward through rotation

**Breaking changes**

- Adds a new nullable authTime column to the oauthRefreshToken table (requires migration)
- Existing refresh tokens will have authTime = NULL, in which case auth_time is omitted from the ID token

Keeps auth_time in ID tokens stable across refresh, per OIDC Core 1.0 §12.2. Captures the original login time and carries it through token rotation so refreshed ID tokens keep the same auth_time.

items.body: Several security-relevant flows read shared state, checked it, then wrote it back in separate steps, so two requests arriving together could each pass the check before either write landed. Depending on the flow, that let a single-use credential be redeemed twice, a counter or quota be pushed past its limit, or a replay marker be created more than once. Rather than add a lock to each route, the affected flows now go through a small set of atomic operations at the storage boundary: consume a single-use record, increment a guarded counter, and reserve a marker first-writer-wins. The new operations (`incrementOne` and `SecondaryStorage.increment` on the adapter contract, `reserveVerificationValue`, and the rate-limit storage's `consume`) are optional and ship with fallbacks, so existing custom adapters and storages keep working unchanged. What it hardens: - Single-use credentials are consumed in one step: two-factor challenges and OTPs, email and phone OTPs, password-reset and delete-account tokens, one-time tokens, the SIWE nonce, device-authorization and Electron codes, and the passkey registration/authentication ceremony. A concurrent or expired replay no longer passes. - Counters and quotas update atomically under a guard: the request rate limiter (now decided entirely on the request, with bounded stores) plus API-key usage and per-key rate limits. A burst can no longer cross the configured limit. - Replay protection: SAML assertion ids are reserved atomically, closing the window where two simultaneous submissions both passed. - Adapter fidelity that the above relies on: memory-adapter transaction isolation and empty-predicate safety, affected-row counts from `updateMany`, surfaced Prisma delete errors, and corrected Bun and Node SQLite driver metadata. - Two smaller gaps: captcha verification is bounded by a timeout, and the Have I Been Pwned check covers the remaining password-setting routes. Secondary-storage-only deployments have no database row to guard, so a few counters and reservations stay best-effort there and log a one-time warning. --- ## Summary by cubic Makes single-use credentials, counters, and replay markers truly atomic to close race windows under concurrent requests. Prevents double redemption, quota/rate-limit overruns, and replay gaps across the API while keeping custom adapters/storages working via fallbacks. - **New Features** - Added `incrementOne` (adapter) and `SecondaryStorage.increment` for guarded, atomic counter updates. Implemented natively in `@better-auth/memory-adapter`, `@better-auth/kysely-adapter`, `@better-auth/drizzle-adapter`, `@better-auth/prisma-adapter`, `@better-auth/mongo-adapter`; `@better-auth/redis-storage` adds `increment`. - Added `reserveVerificationValue` to record single-use markers with first-writer-wins semantics (DB-backed paths are atomic; secondary-storage-only remains best-effort). - Rate-limit storages may implement an optional `consume` for strict, single-step enforcement; without it, legacy behavior is kept with a one-time warning. - **Bug Fixes** - Single-use credentials are consumed atomically across flows: 2FA challenges/OTPs, email/phone OTPs, password-reset and delete-account tokens, one-time tokens, SIWE nonces, device-authorization and Electron codes; passkey challenges are bound to their ceremony and accept a missing marker for in-flight upgrades. - Counters and rate limits update atomically: API-key `remaining` and per-key limits, plus the global request rate limiter (now enforced on request; in-memory store is bounded; DB backend prunes expired entries; opening a fresh window is create-only and real create errors fail fast with a single re-read for true races). - API keys: verification rejects a key whose row disappeared mid-verify, and the in-process reference-list lock no longer leaks entries. - Replay protection is atomic: SAML assertion IDs are reserved so concurrent submissions cannot both pass. - Adapter/driver fidelity: native `incrementOne` now updates at most one row (mirrors `consumeOne`); `incrementOne` honors `mapKeysTransformInput` overrides for increment fields; memory-adapter transactions commit only their delta via a three-way merge and keep empty-predicate safety; Drizzle `updateMany` returns affected-row counts; Kysely SQLite mutation metadata surfaced and MSSQL `consumeOne` fixed; Prisma delete now propagates unexpected errors. - Hardening: captcha verification times out after 10s and fails closed; Have I Been Pwned checks more password-setting routes; accepting team invitations now respects capacity atomically, claims the invitation atomically to prevent duplicate accepts, and marks it accepted only after membership succeeds (failed membership restores the invite to pending). - Tooling: `@better-auth/cli` mock adapter includes `incrementOne`. - Docs: clarified rate-limit `consume` window semantics (sliding on database backends; fixed TTL on secondary storage).
